items.title: Vygotsky's ZPD emphasised social learning
items.claim: Lev Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development (work in 1920s-30s, popularised in West from 1962 onwards) describes:

options.text: The gap between what a child can do alone and what they can do with help from a more knowledgeable other — emphasising social context as constitutive of cognitive development
A physical region of the brain
A stage of motor development only

items.reveal:
Vygotsky died in 1934 aged 37. His work was suppressed in Stalin's USSR and reached the West in translation (Thought and Language, 1962; Mind in Society, 1978).

'Scaffolding' was Bruner's term (Wood, Bruner & Ross 1976) capturing the temporary support that enables a learner to reach beyond independent ability. Modern educational applications: peer tutoring, guided discovery, gradual release of responsibility models.
items.why: Vygotsky's emphasis on social context contrasts with Piaget's relatively solitary child. Modern developmental psychology integrates both — children develop through cultural participation, not despite it.

items.title: Choking is more than just nerves
items.claim: Sian Beilock and colleagues' research on choking under pressure identifies two mechanisms. Which?

options.text: Distraction (anxiety occupies working memory needed for the task) and explicit monitoring (conscious attention to automatic motor skills disrupts them) — different mechanisms suggest different interventions

items.reveal:
Beilock and Carr (2001, 2005) showed expert golfers putted worse when paying conscious attention to their swing; novices benefited from explicit instruction.

Distraction-based choking responds to attention training and pre-performance routines; monitoring-based choking responds to maintaining flow-state distraction (focusing on external targets rather than mechanics). The dual-process model has reshaped elite athlete preparation.
items.why: Choking has identifiable mechanisms with specific countermeasures. Generic 'stay calm' advice misses both.

items.title: Pre-registration commits to analyses before data collection
items.claim: Pre-registration of study designs and analysis plans was adopted by many psychology journals through the 2010s. What problem does it address?

options.text: It distinguishes confirmatory analyses (specified in advance) from exploratory ones (data-driven), preventing post-hoc rationalisation of decisions and reducing the garden of forking paths
It allows researchers to publish without data
It is required by law everywhere

items.reveal:
Registered Reports (introduced at Cortex in 2013, now at 300+ journals) take pre-registration further: methods are peer-reviewed and accepted before data collection, so positive and negative results have equal chance of publication.

Evidence on impact: registered reports show much higher rates of null results being published (Scheel, Schijen & Lakens 2021) and lower effect-size inflation. The OSF (Open Science Framework, 2013) provides infrastructure.
items.why: Pre-registration is a structural fix to publication bias and p-hacking. It separates testing hypotheses from generating them, which conventional analysis blurs.
